diagnostic_evidence.quote: The characterization for $\kappa$-optimally diagonally preconditioned matrix $A$ follows from solving $\nabla \kappa(e)=0$.

Now let $\lambda$ be a singleton eigenvalue of
$\cDo(d)$ with a right eigenvector $x$.

issues.failure_explanation: The characterization "A is kappa-optimally diagonally preconditioned if, and only if, the orthonormal eigenvector pair satisfies x_1 . x_1 = x_n . x_n" is proved only via \nabla\kappa(e)=0, which requires lambda_1 and lambda_n to be singletons (the gradient formula comes from lem:optkappacond, which assumes a singleton eigenvalue). The closing sentence extends the characterization to the nonsmooth case by allowing x_1, x_n to be chosen within the extreme eigenspaces; under that reading the necessity direction is false. Counterexample: A = I + (2/3) e e^T in S^3, with eigenvalues 3 (eigenvector u_1 = e/sqrt(3)) and 1 of multiplicity 2 (eigenspace e^\perp). A is kappa-optimally diagonally preconditioned: a minimizer of kappa(A Diag(d)) exists, and by permutation symmetry of A plus convexity of the optimal set, d=e is optimal (equivalently 0 in the subdifferential of kappa at e, since (1/3,1/3,1/3) lies in conv{x . x : x perp e, ||x||=1}, e.g. the average of the Hadamard squares of (1,-1,0)/sqrt2, (1,0,-1)/sqrt2, (0,1,-1)/sqrt2). But x_1 . x_1 = (1/3,1/3,1/3), and no unit vector x in e^\perp satisfies x . x = (1/3,1/3,1/3): such an x would need entries +/-1/sqrt(3), and no choice of three signs sums to zero. So optimality does not imply existence of a single pair of eigenvectors with equal Hadamard squares; the correct general condition is that the convex hulls of the (normalized) Hadamard squares over the two extreme eigenspaces intersect (i.e. 0 in \partial\kappa(e)), which may require genuine convex combinations.

failure_location.quote:
In the nonsmooth case, we can choose the normalized
$x_1$, respectively, $x_n$, in the eigenspace of 
$\lambda_{\max}(\cDo (d))$, respectively $\lambda_{\min}( \cDo (d))$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the characterization (and the gradient formula) to the case where lambda_1 and lambda_n are singletons, deleting the final sentence or replacing it with the correct nonsmooth condition 0 in \partial\kappa(e), equivalently that the convex hulls of the Hadamard squares over the maximal and minimal eigenspaces intersect.
issues.overall_effect: The necessity direction of the headline if-and-only-if characterization of kappa-optimal diagonal preconditioning is invalid whenever lambda_max or lambda_min has multiplicity greater than one. The gradient formula (with the singleton hypothesis), the smooth-case iff, and the sufficiency direction are unaffected; no downstream result depends on the nonsmooth extension (prop:nonuniqd explicitly assumes singleton eigenpairs, and lem:optAforkappaconstr constructs the singleton case).
issues.title: The if-and-only-if kappa-optimality characterization fails when an extreme eigenvalue has multiplicity greater than one
issues.why_classification: The least repair is a one-line scope restriction to singleton extreme eigenvalues (or a short routine subdifferential restatement). The smooth-case characterization, the sufficiency direction, and every downstream use (prop:nonuniqd, lem:optAforkappaconstr, and the subgradient directions, whose quasisubdifferential membership is proved separately for any eigenvector choice) all survive unchanged, so the loss is confined to the degenerate multiple-eigenvalue case.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: since \Cref{GD} is a subgradient method, in general it is not a descent method.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof invokes Kiwiel's Theorem 1 for quasiconvex subgradient methods with diminishing, non-summable stepsizes, which yields only liminf convergence, liminf_k kappa(oD(d_k)) = kappa_* (equivalently, convergence of the running minimum). The clause "in particular, kappa(oD(d_k)) \downarrow kappa_*" asserts monotone decrease of the objective sequence itself. This does not follow from liminf convergence and is false in general: the paper itself states that Algorithm GD is not a descent method, and subgradient iterations with decaying stepsizes generate oscillating objective values. The running minimum kappa_*^j = min_{k=1}^j kappa(oD(d_k)) is defined in the statement but never used, indicating the intended (and valid) claim was kappa_*^j \downarrow kappa_*, which is exactly equivalent to the liminf statement.

failure_location.quote:
It then holds that $\underline{\lim}_{k \rightarrow \infty} \kappa(\cDo(d_k))=\kappa_{*}$; 
 in particular, $\kappa(\cDo(d_k))\downarrow \kappa_{*}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace "kappa(oD(d_k)) \downarrow kappa_*" with the running-minimum statement kappa_*^j \downarrow kappa_* (using the already-defined quantity), or delete the "in particular" clause, keeping the liminf conclusion.
issues.overall_effect: The theorem overstates its convergence guarantee: only liminf (best-iterate) convergence of Algorithm GD is established, while the asserted monotone convergence of the objective values to kappa_* is unsupported and generally false. No other result or guarantee builds on the monotone claim (the nonasymptotic result thm:Nonasymptotic Theorem concerns the separate compact formulation and is proved independently).
issues.title: Theorem 2.4 asserts monotone convergence kappa(oD(d_k)) downarrow kappa_* that the proof does not establish and that is false in general
issues.why_classification: A one-line correction using the running minimum already defined in the statement preserves the substantive asymptotic guarantee (liminf convergence to kappa_*) and no downstream claim depends on the false monotonicity assertion.
